live.name: BRONZE SATIN
live.headline: BRONZE SATIN: what the catalogue records about this tracked threat actor
live.in_short: BRONZE SATIN is Secureworks' name for an actor also tracked as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon. The catalogue lists two web shell tools. No report card gives more detail.

sentences.t: BRONZE SATIN is the name used in the Secureworks entry for this threat actor.
The catalogue lists three other names for the same actor: HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
The catalogue lists two tools for this actor: ChinaChopper and Godzilla Webshell.

next.headline: BRONZE SATIN (HAFNIUM, Silk Typhoon): Exchange zero-days and a shift to IT supply chains
next.in_short: BRONZE SATIN, also tracked as HAFNIUM and Silk Typhoon, is an espionage actor. Microsoft calls it Chinese and state-run. It is known for the 2021 Exchange attacks and, later, for going after IT supply chains.

sentences.t: BRONZE SATIN is the Secureworks name for a group also tracked as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes Silk Typhoon as an espionage-focused Chinese state actor. Microsoft says it began tracking the group in 2020.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre judges it highly likely that HAFNIUM is associated with the Chinese state.

Italian media (ANSA), as relayed by BleepingComputer, reported that Xu Zewei was arrested in Milan on a U.S. warrant. The report says Xu is allegedly linked to Silk Typhoon and does not confirm the link. No extradition decision is reported.
Microsoft says victims of the group's recent supply-chain activity were largely in state and local government and the IT sector.
BleepingComputer reports the group has attacked defense contractors, policy think tanks, NGOs, healthcare, law firms and higher education in the United States, Australia, Japan and Vietnam.
Italian media link Silk Typhoon to 2020 attacks on infectious disease researchers and healthcare organisations seeking anti-COVID vaccine data. The BleepingComputer report does not confirm this.
The catalogue lists two web shells among the group's tools: China Chopper and Godzilla Webshell.
China Chopper is a web shell of about 4 kilobytes, first discovered in 2012. A Wikipedia article says Hafnium used a JScript version of it in 2021 against Exchange Server.
Microsoft reports that Silk Typhoon uses stolen API keys to reach the customers of IT providers. It also uses password spray, zero-day exploits, and abuse of OAuth applications.
Microsoft says the group is not known to use its own dedicated infrastructure. It typically relies on compromised covert networks, proxies and VPNs, likely to obscure its operations.
On March 2, 2021, Microsoft reported HAFNIUM exploiting four zero-days in Exchange Server, according to Kaspersky.
Elastic saw webshells, credential harvesting, mailbox theft and new accounts in the Exchange activity. It cautioned that some of it may have come from opportunistic threats rather than HAFNIUM.
The UK said the early-2021 Exchange compromise affected over a quarter of a million servers. The NCSC called it almost certain that a Chinese state-backed actor was behind it.

In December 2022, the U.S. and allies attributed the Exchange campaign to hackers affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security. Microsoft had earlier assessed with high confidence that HAFNIUM was exploiting the flaws.
Microsoft says that in 2024 Silk Typhoon used zero-days in Citrix NetScaler and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect. It says the group exploited an Ivanti VPN zero-day in January 2025.

BleepingComputer, citing Bloomberg and unnamed sources, linked Silk Typhoon to a December hack of the U.S. Treasury's OFAC. The attackers reportedly used a stolen BeyondTrust API key. The attribution rests on those sources, not on the outlet's own finding.
Patch internet-facing servers and edge devices quickly. Guard and rotate API keys for remote support and management tools.
